title: Routing latency surge — handheld investigation notes
body:
Top-line: quick scratchpad from the field while chasing a late-night latency spike that turned into partial regional failover. Primary symptom: elevated p50/p95 for text-gen calls routed to eu-west-1; some requests falling back to a slower variant in eu-central-1, causing client-visible 1s+ tail latency.

Observed at ~2026-02-17 22:43 UTC. Alerts: routing-slo-eu-west1-p95, model-fallback-rate-increase.

Environment/context:
- Hosted API (default smart-routing policy: latency-first, prefer-local-region:true)
- Model catalog: gptx-7b-q4f (primary in eu-west-1), gptx-7b-q4f-compat (fallback in eu-central-1), gptx-7b-8bit (cold in us-west-2 for capacity overflow)
- Autoscaling target for eu-west-1 service: 220 tokens/sec per GPU; pool temporarily at 75% due to scheduled maintenance on some nodes (was not in calendar).

Raw timeline (notes as I scribbled):
- 22:42:36 - first p95 alert (0.9s -> 1.6s)
- 22:43:01 - spike escalates; increase in fallback_count metric (route.fallback.invocations)
- 22:45:10 - manual quick-check of metrics dashboards: CPU/GPU load shows patchy high driver utilization on subset of hosts (az1-equivalent in eu-west-1)
- 22:48:00 - started hunting in logs + tried traffic steering toggle to force local-only routing for small canary (no effect)
- 22:52:12 - temporary mitigation: pinned a handful of tenants to eu-central-1 (reduced latency for those tenants but increased cross-region egress for many)

Commands I ran (copied from history):
- curl to reproduce from local workstation (shows ~1.5s):
  curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer xxxxx" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?model=gptx-7b-q4f" -d '{"prompt":"hello"}'

- curl with --trace-time to see connection stages:
  curl --trace-time -v -H "Authorization: Bearer xxxxx" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?model=gptx-7b-q4f" -d '{"prompt":"test"}' 2>&1 | sed -n '1,120p'
  // result: DNS/CONNECT fine, TLS handshake fine, long wait after POST until first byte (server processing + fallback hop)

- kubectl on node with suspected high driver usage:
  kubectl -n serving get pods -l pool=eu-west-1 -o wide | grep gpu
  kubectl -n serving logs pod/inf-serve-abc -c infer-runtime --tail=200 | grep KVCacheMiss -n

- ssh and nvidia-smi snapshot (I scp'd a screenshot):
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1 -f /tmp/gpu-snapshot.csv

- quick redis / cache probe (prefix cache behavior):
  redis-cli -h cache-eu-west-1.get --eval 'GET prefix:e2e:abc'
  // many cold misses during spike -> increases token generation work

Key log snippets (sanitized):
- infer-runtime logs: 2026-02-17T22:44:12Z ERROR route-manager: fallback triggered: target=eu-west-1 variant=gptx-7b-q4f reason=capacity-exhausted token_stream_id=xxxx
- orbit-router: WARN 2026-02-17T22:44:15Z route-eval: preference_score changed: {eu-west-1:0.72, eu-central-1:0.84} -> decision: route to eu-central-1 (compat)
- proxy: 2026-02-17T22:45:03Z 503 POST /v1/generate 10.1.12.45:429 -> 10.2.5.78:503 connection reset by peer
- serving-runtime: 2026-02-17T22:46:21Z DEBUG KVCacheMiss prefix:e2e:abc key=3f4d

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Local capacity exhaustion + high cold cache miss rate caused latency to spike; smart-routing policy saw eu-central-1 with slightly better latency and started fallbacking. Fallback hop added cross-region transfer and model-variant mismatch overhead -> exacerbated tail latency.
2) A subset of GPUs in eu-west-1 had driver-level throttling (observed temp spikes + occasional process restarts) causing intermittent pod restarts and transient capacity loss.
3) Network blips between control plane region and compute nodes (some 503s show connection reset) causing the router to over-correct routing scores.
4) Regression in preference score calculation: weight on recent latency is overly aggressive (half-life too short), causing thrashy routing decisions when a small fraction of servers hiccup.

Things tried and results:
- traffic-steering toggle (force-local for a tiny canary): no improvement for broader traffic because fallback already engaged at upstream router layer.
- manual scale up nodes in eu-west-1 (provisioned + warmed): p95 decreased gradually after new capacity came online (~10 minutes).
- pinned tenants to eu-central-1: improved for those tenants but client metrics showed more variability due to increased RTT.
- purged local prefix cache for a few keys (simulate cold starts): increased cost but latency lowered once cache warmed for a minute.

Data pointers to check (what to pull next):
- route score time series for the affected 20 minutes (metric: router.preference_score.{region})
- pod lifecycle events in eu-west-1 between 22:30-23:00 (kube events)
- kernel/syslog on nodes with restarts (OOM? driver crash?)
- traceroutes for failing connections (we saw some RSTs)
- compare KV cache hit rate before/during/after spike (metric: kvcache.hit_rate per pool)
- recent commits to routing policy calculator (PRs touching decay/half-life)

Short config snippet I had open (note — local copy of policy, not exact production):
policy: 
  routing_priority: [latency, cost]
  latency_window_sec: 60
  half_life_sec: 15  
  prefer_local: true
  fallback_order: [same_model_variant, compat_variant, remote_region]

Potential fixes / mitigations (short-term -> long-term):
- short term: increase min capacity buffer in eu-west-1 during maintenance windows; temporarily lengthen half-life to avoid thrashing during small blips (experiment on canary).
- medium: change fallback_order to prefer same_model_variant in remote region before switching to compat variant (compat increases serialization/deserialization overhead).
- medium: add hysteresis to preference score changes (require N consecutive windows to flip region preference).
- medium/long: improve prefix/KV cache replication across nearby regions or add a warm-up step during failover to avoid cold-cache penalties.
- long: deeper investigation into GPU driver crashes and node stability; replace/retire problematic instance types.

Open questions / TODOs (my action list):
- grab core dump (if exists) from suspect driver crash node (ask sRE on call to collect).
- extract exact timeline of router decisions: who flipped preference at 22:44:15? correlate with node restart event.
- run offline simulation of routing policy with synthetic short blip to measure flip rate (work with eng-observability).
- propose temporary guardrail: don't downgrade to compat variant automatically unless local latency > X and capacity < Y for T seconds.

Notes for follow-ups:
- Slack trail: #inc-rt-2147 (thread has some console snippets)
- I pushed a tiny canary change to routing config on staging (pr: github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/3333) to test increased half-life.

Misc scribbles/less-structured thoughts:
- fallback is doing the right thing in presence of sustained local capacity loss, but our thresholds/penalties make the system overly reactive to microbursts. We should treat model-variant compatibility penalty explicitly in scoring function (e.g., add 100ms fixed penalty for compat variant).
- consider adding a per-tenant sticky-preference TTL so a tenant doesn't bounce regions during a short outage.
- check whether dedicated-reserved capacity customers were impacted — if so, we need to review SLA routing overrides.

If I get time tomorrow:
- correlate p99 requests with trace IDs to see how many hops/fallbacks were in each trace (how many cross-region redirects).
- flesh out a one-pager with recommended short-term guardrails for the on-call rotation to apply during maintenance windows.

End of notes (saved as-is).
